reflection_question: Where do you feel most unseen right now - and what would change if you believed God was there specifically?
devotional_text:
Yesterday you handed over the last part.

Today we start the second part of the sixty days, and it is about who God actually is when He finds you.

Not who you fear He is. Who He has shown Himself to be, over and over, to people in far worse positions than yours.

We start with a slave girl in a desert.

# Nobody Was Looking For Her

Hagar was an Egyptian servant in Abraham's household. She had no standing, no choice and no power.

Sarai could not have children, so Hagar was given to Abraham to produce one. When she became pregnant, the household turned on her, and she was treated so harshly that she ran into the wilderness.

A pregnant foreign slave, alone, in a desert, with nowhere to go.

Nobody in that story is coming after her. There is no search party. She is, by every measure that counted in her world, a person who could disappear without anyone minding much.

## And Then

> "Yahweh's angel found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness." (Genesis 16:7)

**Found her.**

Which means somebody was looking.

The first person in the whole Bible to be met by the angel of the Lord is not a patriarch or a prophet or a king. It is a pregnant runaway slave girl that everybody else had finished with.

That is not an accident. That is God telling you something about where He goes.

## The Question He Asks

> "Hagar, Sarai's servant, where did you come from? Where are you going?" (Genesis 16:8)

He uses her name.

In the chapter up to this point, Sarai and Abram have been talking about her, and they never once say it. She is "my servant." An object in somebody else's plan.

God says *Hagar*.

And He asks her two questions He already knows the answers to — the same thing He did in the garden. Where have you come from, where are you going.

He is not gathering information. He is giving her the dignity of speaking for herself, probably for the first time in years.

## She Answers Honestly

> "I am fleeing from the face of my mistress Sarai." (Genesis 16:8)

She only answers the first question.

She can say where she is running from. She has no idea where she is running to.

That is where a lot of people in this fight live. You know exactly what you are trying to get away from. You could not tell anybody where you are heading.

God does not scold her for the half answer.

## What She Calls Him

After everything, she gives God a name. The first person in Scripture ever to do so, and it is her.

> "She called the name of Yahweh who spoke to her, 'You are a God who sees.'" (Genesis 16:13)

Not *a God who rescued me from the situation*. He actually sends her back into a hard place.

Not *a God who fixed it*.

**A God who sees.**

That was what she had been starving for. Not an outcome. Being seen by somebody who mattered, as a person with a name, in the worst week of her life.

## Why This Is Day Eleven

Because one of the quiet agonies of addiction is being unseen.

The people around you see a version. The functional one, or the difficult one, or the disappointing one. Almost nobody sees the whole picture — how hard you are actually fighting, how many times you have nearly said something, what it takes just to get through an ordinary Thursday.

And so you conclude that nobody is looking.

**Hagar concluded the same thing, in a desert, and was wrong.**

## What To Watch For In Genesis 16

* 🗣️ How Abram and Sarai refer to Hagar, and what they never call her
* 🏜️ Where the angel finds her — not at home, in the wilderness
* 📛 The first word out of the angel's mouth in verse 8
* ❓ The two questions, and that she only answers one
* 🔙 That God sends her back, rather than removing the hardship
* 👁️ The name she gives Him in verse 13

## The Bigger Takeaway

God does not wait for you to get back to the house before He will deal with you.

He goes into the desert, uses your name, asks you where you are going, and does not flinch at the answer.

**Being seen is not the same as being fixed.** He did not fix Hagar's circumstances that day. He gave her something she needed more: proof that she was not invisible, and a promise about her future.

That is worth more on a bad day than most of the advice you have been given.

## Today's One Thing

**Answer His two questions, out loud.**

*Where have you come from?*

Say the honest version. What you are running from. What happened, or what keeps happening, or what you cannot stand to feel.

*Where are you going?*

And if the honest answer is "I have no idea," say that. Hagar did. It was accepted.

Then say the name back to Him: *You are a God who sees.*

If you do not believe it yet, say it anyway. Some things you have to say for a while before they land.

## Today's Prayer

God,

I have felt invisible for a long time.

People see the parts of me I let them see. Even the ones who love me do not know what this actually takes, and I have made sure of that.

You went into a desert for a woman that nobody was looking for, and You used her name.

Use mine.

I can tell You what I am running from. I cannot tell You where I am going. I am hoping that is enough to start with.

You are a God who sees. Please see me here.

In Jesus' name, amen.

reflection_question: Whose voice is the loudest accuser in your head? Is it actually somebody else's voice, or has it become your own?
devotional_text:
There is a scene in John's gospel that people quote constantly and usually only half remember.

It is worth reading properly, because the full version is better than the famous line.

# How It Starts

A woman is dragged into the temple court in the morning and put in the middle of a circle of men.

She has been caught in adultery. The text says *in the very act*, which tells you how she arrived there — pulled out of a room, probably half dressed, in front of a crowd.

There is a detail the religious leaders are quietly not mentioning. The law they are citing required both people to be brought. There is no man in this scene.

So she is not really the point. She is the instrument. They want to trap Jesus, and she is what they picked up to do it with.

**Being used as somebody else's weapon, while your worst moment is read out in public.** That is where this starts.

## He Does Not Answer

He bends down and writes on the ground.

Nobody knows what He wrote. People have guessed for two thousand years. What matters is what it did: it broke the staring.

For a moment, every eye in that circle went to the dirt instead of to her.

Then, when they keep pushing:

> "He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her." (John 8:7)

And He bends down and writes again.

## They Leave In Order

> "They, when they heard it, being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last." (John 8:9)

Beginning from the oldest.

The ones who had lived longest understood first. They had more years of knowing what was in them.

One by one, the circle empties.

## Then The Two Sentences

> "Jesus was left alone with the woman where she was, in the middle." (John 8:9)

Left alone with her. In the middle.

The only person present with the standing to condemn her is the only person left.

> "Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you?" She said, "No one, Lord." Jesus said, "Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more." (John 8:10-11)

Read both halves, because almost everybody only keeps one.

**"Neither do I condemn you."** That is first. Before any instruction, before any change, before she has promised anything.

**"From now on, sin no more."** That is second. Not a condition of the first. A consequence of it.

People who want to be harsh quote the second half. People who want to avoid change quote the first. He said both, in that order, and the order is the message.

## Why The Order Matters For You

You have been trying to do this the other way round for years.

*First I will stop. Then I will be able to face God. Then maybe I will be forgiven and feel something other than disgust when I pray.*

It does not work. Nobody has ever managed it, because the thing you are trying to stop is largely fed by the shame you are carrying while you try.

Jesus goes first. The condemnation is dealt with before the instruction is given. She walks out of that circle already not condemned, and *then* she goes and lives differently.

**You do not clean yourself up to come to Him. You come to Him and that is where the cleaning happens.**

## What To Watch For In John 8:1-11

* ⚖️ Who is missing from the scene, given what the law they cite actually required
* ✍️ That Jesus writes on the ground twice, and what it does to the crowd
* 🧓 The order in which they leave, in verse 9
* 🎯 Where she is standing when everybody has gone
* 1️⃣ Which of Jesus' two sentences comes first

## The Bigger Takeaway

There is a circle around you too.

Some of the voices are real people. Most of them are not any more — they are recordings, playing in your own voice, of things somebody said to you a long time ago.

In the story, the accusers leave and Jesus stays.

That is the right picture to carry: **when every other voice has gone quiet, the one left standing with you is the one who refuses to condemn you.**

## Today's One Thing

**Identify the voice.**

When you fail, something speaks. Today, notice whose voice it actually is.

A parent? A teacher? Somebody from church? An ex? Yourself at nineteen?

Write the name if there is one.

Then write the sentence it says, and underneath it write John 8:11, in full, in your own handwriting:

*Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.*

Two sentences from two different sources. One of them is God's. Learn which.

## Today's Prayer

Jesus,

There is a circle around me most days, and it has been there so long I thought it was just what thinking sounded like.

I have been trying to earn my way back to You. Get clean first, then come. And I never get clean, so I never come.

You told her she was not condemned before she had changed one thing.

I need You to say it to me, because I cannot say it to myself and make it stick.

And when You say "go and sin no more" — I want that. I do. Not to keep You. Because You already stayed.

Stand in the middle with me.

In Your name, amen.

day_title: Shame And Conviction Are Not The Same Thing
reflection_question: Think of the last time you felt terrible about this. Did it push you toward God or away from Him? What does that tell you about where it came from?
devotional_text:
Two things feel almost identical from the inside and do completely opposite work.

One of them is from God. One of them will keep you exactly where you are until the day you die.

If you learn nothing else in these sixty days, learn to tell them apart.

# Paul Names Them

> "For godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world produces death." (2 Corinthians 7:10)

Two sorrows. Same feeling, opposite destinations.

One produces repentance — a turning, a change of direction, and no regret afterwards.

The other produces death.

That is strong language and he means it. Not hell. *Death* — the slow kind. Giving up. Deciding this is simply who you are. Shrinking.

## How To Tell Them Apart

There is a simple test and it works almost every time.

**Conviction is about what you did. Shame is about what you are.**

* ⚡ Conviction says: *that was wrong, and it hurt people, and it is not who you are meant to be.*
* 🕳️ Shame says: *you are disgusting. Of course you did that. It is what you are.*

And then watch the direction they push you.

* 🏃 Conviction moves you **toward** God. It is painful and it comes with a door in it.
* 🚪 Shame moves you **away** from God. It makes the idea of praying feel absurd.

That second test is the giveaway. **God never, ever convicts you in a way that makes you want to avoid Him.** That is not how He works. Conviction always has an invitation inside it.

If what you are feeling has no door in it, it did not come from God, however religious it sounds.

## Why This Matters So Much Here

Because shame is not neutral in this fight. It is fuel.

Here is the loop, and you will recognise it:

1. You use.
2. You feel disgusting.
3. Feeling disgusting is unbearable.
4. You reach for the thing that makes unbearable feelings go away.
5. Which is the thing.

Shame does not stop the behaviour. **Shame is one of the main triggers for it.**

So all those years of beating yourself up, believing that if you were just hard enough on yourself you would finally stop — that was not discipline. That was pouring petrol on it.

## What Paul Is Actually Writing About

The context matters. Paul had written the Corinthians a hard letter. It hurt them.

And he says something surprising about it:

> "I now rejoice, not that you were made sorry, but that you were made sorry to repentance." (2 Corinthians 7:9)

He is not glad they felt bad. He is glad it *went somewhere*.

That is the measure. Not the intensity of the feeling. Where it took them.

You can feel appalling for a decade and go nowhere. Many people do.

## A Hard Question

Some people reading this have confused feeling terrible with doing something.

The self-hatred becomes a kind of substitute penance. *I may not have changed, but look how much I hate myself about it — surely that counts for something.*

It does not count for anything. It is not repentance. It is just suffering that leaves everything where it was.

Godly sorrow has hands and feet. It makes a call. It tells somebody. It pours it away. It books the appointment.

## What To Watch For In 2 Corinthians 7:5-13

* 😣 How honest Paul is about his own distress in verse 5
* 💬 What comforted him, in verse 6 — it is a person arriving
* ⚖️ The two sorrows in verse 10, and the two destinations
* 🔧 The list in verse 11 of what godly sorrow *produced* — all of it active
* 🚫 "Which brings no regret" — godly sorrow does not leave a residue

## The Bigger Takeaway

You have probably believed that the self-loathing was the godly part of you.

It is not. It is the thing that has been keeping the cycle turning.

**God's conviction is sharp, specific, and always has a way out of it. Shame is vague, total, and has no exit.**

Learning to hear the difference is one of the most practical skills in recovery, and it is in the Bible, written to a church that had made a mess.

## Today's One Thing

**Sort your last episode.**

Think about the last time you failed at this, and the feeling that came afterwards.

Write down what the feeling actually said. The words.

Then ask the two questions:

1. Is this about something I **did**, or about what I **am**?
2. Did it move me **toward** God or **away** from Him?

If it was about what you are, and it pushed you away — that was not God, and you can stop treating it as His voice.

And then do the thing conviction would have told you to do. One specific action. The call, the deletion, the confession, the appointment.

**Feeling bad is not the work. Turning is the work.**

## Today's Prayer

God,

I have spent years thinking that hating myself about this was the same as repenting.

It was not. It never changed anything. It just made the next time more likely, because I could not stand being in my own head and I knew exactly how to get out of it for an hour.

Teach me the difference between Your voice and the other one.

I am asking for the sharp, specific, honest kind of sorrow. The kind that has a door in it.

And take the other thing off me. The flat, heavy, permanent verdict I have been carrying about what I am.

You never told me that. I want to stop repeating it as though You did.

In Jesus' name, amen.

reflection_question: What part of this do you believe would make people pull away if they knew? Say that specific thing to God today.
devotional_text:
There is a short scene in Mark that lasts three verses and answers a question you have probably never said out loud.

The question is: *would He actually want to?*

Not *could* He. You mostly believe He could.

Would He want to, knowing what I actually am.

# What Leprosy Meant

It was not only a disease. It was a sentence.

Under the law, a leper lived outside the camp. They could not be touched. They could not worship with everybody else. If somebody came near, they had to call out a warning so people could get away from them.

Years of that. Decades, sometimes.

So picture what it does to a person. Not just the illness — **the certainty that you are contaminating, and that anyone decent should keep their distance.**

If any of that is familiar, you understand this man better than most readers do.

## What He Says

> "A leper came to him, begging him, kneeling down to him, and saying to him, 'If you want to, you can make me clean.'" (Mark 1:40)

Stop at that sentence, because it is extraordinary.

He has no doubt about the power. *You can make me clean.* That is settled in his mind.

What he does not know is whether Jesus would *want* to.

**If you want to.**

That is the question of somebody who has been told for years that he is repulsive and has started to agree.

And it is your question. You believe God could get you out of this. What you are not sure about is whether He still wants to, after this many times.

## What Jesus Does Before He Speaks

> "Being moved with compassion, he stretched out his hand, and touched him." (Mark 1:41)

He touched him.

He did not need to. He healed plenty of people with a word, at a distance, including people He never met.

He could have cleaned him first and then embraced him. That would have been the sensible order.

**He touched him while he was still a leper.**

That man had not felt human contact in years. Whatever the healing meant to him, I suspect the hand came first.

## And Then The Three Words

> "I want to. Be made clean." (Mark 1:41)

He answers the exact question that was asked.

The man said *if You want to*. Jesus said **I want to**.

Not "I suppose so." Not "this is the last time." Not a lecture about how he got there.

I want to.

## Why This Is The Day Fourteen Question

Because there is something in your story you believe would end it.

Not the general shape of the addiction — you have half admitted that to a few people. The specific thing. What you did to get it, or what you did while on it, or what you have let happen, or who you have become at three in the morning.

You have decided that if God saw *that* specific thing clearly, something would change in how He feels about you.

The leper thought the same. He was wrong about the one thing he was most certain of.

## What To Watch For In Mark 1:35-45

* 🌄 What Jesus does before the crowds in verse 35 — He goes out alone to pray
* 🙇 The posture of the man in verse 40
* ❓ The exact wording of his request — what he doubts and what he does not
* ✋ That the touch comes before the healing
* 🗣️ That Jesus answers the man's actual question, word for word

## The Bigger Takeaway

You can believe God is powerful and still believe He is reluctant about you.

That combination is one of the loneliest places a person can live, and it is exactly where this man was standing.

**I want to.**

That is not a sentence about what God is capable of. It is a sentence about what He is like.

## Today's One Thing

**Say the specific thing.**

Not "my addiction." The detail. The one you have been keeping back even in the last four days of honesty, because it is the part that would change how somebody looked at you.

Say it to God, plainly, and then ask the leper's question in your own words:

*If You want to, You can make me clean.*

Then sit still and let the answer be what it is. Do not rush past it.

**I want to.**

If you cannot feel that today, write it down anyway and read it tomorrow. Some sentences take a few mornings to get in.

## Today's Prayer

Jesus,

I have never really doubted that You could.

I have doubted that You would still want to, by now, with this specific thing, after this many times of me coming back and saying the same words.

I feel like something people should keep a distance from. I have started agreeing with it.

You reached out and touched a man that nobody had touched in years, before anything about him had changed.

Do that here.

Not from a distance. Not after I am better.

Now, as I am.

In Your name, amen.

reflection_question: When did you last sleep properly and eat properly? What is one physical thing you could fix this week?
devotional_text:
This may be the most practical day in the whole sixty, and it is about a prophet who wanted to die.

If you are exhausted today, read this one slowly.

# The Timing Is The Strange Part

Elijah has just had the greatest day of his career.

He stood alone against four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel. Fire came down from heaven in front of the whole nation. He outran a chariot.

And then the queen sends one threatening message, and he runs for his life into the desert and asks God to kill him.

> "It is enough. Now, O Yahweh, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers." (1 Kings 19:4)

**The crash comes after the victory, not during the battle.**

Anybody who has strung together a good run and then fallen apart in week three knows that pattern precisely. You hold it together through the crisis. It is afterwards, when the pressure drops, that you go down.

## What God Does First

This is the part that should change how you treat yourself.

God does not rebuke him. God does not remind him about the fire on the mountain. God does not give him a verse.

> "He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, 'Arise and eat!' He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again." (1 Kings 19:5-6)

Sleep. Then food. Then **more sleep**.

And then, a second time:

> "Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you." (1 Kings 19:7)

The journey is too great for you. Not a criticism — a diagnosis. *You do not have enough in you for what is ahead, so eat.*

The first thing heaven sent the suicidal prophet was a nap and a hot meal, twice, before a single word of theology.

## Why This Is In A Study About Addiction

Because an enormous amount of relapse is physical and nobody tells you.

You are not weak at 11 p.m. because your faith is shallow. You are weak at 11 p.m. because you are exhausted, you have eaten badly, you have not been outside, and your body is screaming for relief from something and will take whatever is nearest.

There is a phrase used in recovery rooms for exactly this. **Hungry, angry, lonely, tired.** Check those four before you trust any decision you are about to make.

It is not spiritual advice. It is Elijah under the tree, and God agreed with it.

## Then God Speaks

After the sleep and the food and a long journey, God asks him a question — twice — and lets him complain the whole way through it.

And then comes the famous bit. A great wind, an earthquake, a fire. God is not in any of them.

> "After the fire, there was a still small voice." (1 Kings 19:12)

The man who had just called down literal fire from heaven needed to learn that God is usually not in the spectacular thing.

If you are waiting for a dramatic deliverance — a moment where it lifts and never comes back — understand that it almost never arrives that way. It is usually the still small voice, sixty ordinary mornings in a row.

## And One More Thing

Elijah twice says: *I am the only one left.*

God corrects him at the very end.

> "Yet I reserved seven thousand in Israel, all the knees of which have not bowed to Baal." (1 Kings 19:18)

Seven thousand. He thought he was alone and he was wrong by seven thousand.

That was Day 9, and here it is again from a different direction. The feeling of being the only one is extremely convincing and extremely unreliable.

## What To Watch For In 1 Kings 19:1-18

* 📉 What has just happened before verse 1, and how fast he crashes
* 😴 The order of what the angel provides in verses 5 to 7
* 🔁 That the food comes twice, because once was not enough
* 🗣️ The question God asks in verse 9, and that He asks it again in verse 13
* 🌬️ Where God is not, in verses 11 and 12
* 7️⃣ The number in verse 18

## The Bigger Takeaway

Some of what you have been treating as a spiritual failure is a sleep problem.

Some of it is a food problem, or an isolation problem, or a Sunday-afternoon-with-nothing-to-do problem.

That is not a lesser diagnosis. **God treated the body first and the soul second, in that order, for His own prophet.**

You are allowed to do the same. Looking after yourself physically is not a distraction from the real work. On a lot of days, it *is* the real work.

## Today's One Thing

**Fix one physical thing this week.**

Pick one. Not five.

* 🛏️ A bedtime. An actual one, with an alarm to tell you to go.
* 🍽️ Eating before the hard hour, not after it.
* 💧 Water next to the bed.
* 🚶 Twenty minutes outside, daylight on your face.
* 📵 The phone charging in a different room.

Write down which one, and when it starts.

And tonight, before you trust any strong feeling, run the four: **hungry, angry, lonely, tired.** If two or more are true, that feeling is not telling you the truth about your life. It is telling you about your body.

## Today's Prayer

God,

I am so tired, and I have been treating that as a character flaw.

I have asked You a hundred times to make me stronger, and I have never once asked You to help me sleep.

You sent Your prophet a meal and a bed before You sent him a word. You said the journey was too great for him, and You did not say it to shame him.

Say it to me. Let me hear it as kindness.

Help me take care of this body You gave me, as part of the fight and not as a distraction from it.

And when I am waiting for something dramatic, remind me that You are usually in the quiet, ordinary, unremarkable morning.

I will take the still small voice. Just do not go quiet altogether.

In Jesus' name, amen.
